conventions: Distributive ish ish in the casuistic protasis (17.3, 17.8, 17.10, 17.13): the first token takes the lexical 'man' together with the construction-supplied existential frame 'there be' (rule 20), and the repetition, which is what makes the phrase distributive, takes the quantifier - 'What ... soever' in 17.3, discontinuous under rule 25, and 'Whatsoever'/'whatsoever' elsewhere. The reverse assignment of the two identical tokens is defensible and is named in each unit's note. This governs only the case where the ASV writes both a quantifier and a noun; where it renders the pair by a single expression the corpus puts that expression on the first token (LEV.15.2 'any man'; EXO.36.4, EZK.14.4, EZK.14.7 'every'), and those units are not evidence against this reading.

A copular or resumptive pronoun written in a tripartite nominal clause takes the ASV's 'is' (17.11 hi' and hu', 17.14 hu' and hi'), on the principle the contract uses elsewhere that a present morpheme takes its English before the construction supplies one; the preposition or predicate noun keeps only its own English ('in the blood', 'all one with', 'the blood thereof'). Where no such pronoun stands, the supplied copula joins the predicate as usual: 17.2 gives 'This' to zeh and 'is ... thing' to ha-dabar. The competing reading - copula to the prepositional predicate under rule 49 or to the predicate noun under rule 20, with the pronoun unrepresented under rule 22 - is named in each unit's note and is what the corpus mostly does: hu'/hi' is aligned to a bare 'is' in two units (1KI.20.3; 1KI.8.41, hedged) against 65 marked unrepresented as resumptive subjects. Nothing was promoted to the contract on this, and a later chapter may settle it the other way.
report: Checked all 35 candidate lemma groups and, because the table is blind to added units, read the sixteen verse dumps end to end against their six added units. No construction is analysed two ways without a source or ASV licence, so patches is empty.

Uniform across the chapter: the distributive ish ish (17.3, 17.8, 17.10, 17.13); ha + hu' fused on the single 'that' with the article on ish unrepresented (17.4 twice, 17.9); be-tokh -> 'among' under rule 30 (17.8, 17.10, 17.12, 17.13); kol + lo' fused on one 'no' under rule 35 (17.12, 17.14); rule 33 prepositions supplied for bare nominals ('as an oblation' 17.4, 'for sacrifices' 17.5, 'at the door' 17.6, 'in hunting' 17.13); supplied object pronouns added under rule 44 (17.3, 17.4, 17.16); object markers unrepresented with the pronoun on their suffix (17.5, 17.9, 17.10).

Candidates that are not splits, with what licenses each: petach takes a supplied 'at' only in 17.6, the one occurrence with no 'el standing before it, and takes only 'the door' in 17.4, 17.5 and 17.9 where the preposition holds the 'unto'; the apodosis waw is aligned where the ASV writes a connective ('and' 17.4, 'then' 17.15 and 17.16) and unrepresented where it writes none (17.9, 17.10, 17.13, 17.15); kol takes the determiner 'any' where it stands on the noun (17.10) while a supplied 'any' joins the noun where no kol stands (17.13), which is rule 15's limit read in both directions; the assimilated article takes the demonstrative 'that' in 17.10 because no other morpheme competes for the phrase's one determiner, and takes nothing in 17.4 and 17.9 where ha-hu' does; le before an infinitive is unrepresented in le'mor (17.1, 17.2) and takes the written 'to' in 17.4, 17.9 and 17.11.

Supplied English was checked verse by verse, since the lemma table cannot see it, and the chapter holds one boundary throughout: a supplied word joins the morpheme whose own construction licenses it (the existential 'there be' on the first ish, the copula on a predicate, 'manner of' on the noun in 17.10 and 17.14, the indefinite article on its noun, 'that which dieth of itself' on the anarthrous substantives of 17.15 under rule 46), and is added where no morpheme answers for it ('it'/'them' 17.3, 17.4, 17.16; 'as to' 17.14; the cleft 'that' 17.11; the subject 'he' 17.15). The two relative-pronoun treatments do not collide: 17.15's are rule 46 substantives with no antecedent, 17.11's cleft has a written antecedent, which rule 46 excludes in terms.

BSB: all 14 disagreements are documented convention differences and none is a genuine error. Rule 27 on the le of le'mor (17.1, 17.2); rule 40 on prepositions the ASV's recasting leaves nothing to say (the le after michuts in 17.3, the two be of 'whether he be home born or a sojourner' in 17.15); rule 16 on the object markers of 17.5 and 17.9, whose suffixes carry the pronoun; rule 41's determiner count on ha'ish hahu' (17.4, 17.9); rule 14 on the four apodosis waws the ASV leaves unwritten (17.9, 17.10, 17.13, 17.15); and rule 22 on the resumptive suffix of 'achareihem in 17.7, where 'after which' is two words and so is not a rule 30 fusion.

The chapter's most contestable judgment, which I logged rather than rewrote: a written copular pronoun in a tripartite nominal clause takes the ASV's 'is' (17.11 twice, 17.14 twice), while a clause without one gives the supplied copula to the predicate (17.2). The corpus I asked for leans the other way - hu'/hi' is aligned to a bare 'is' in two units (1KI.20.3; 1KI.8.41, hedged) against 65 marked unrepresented as resumptive subjects - and rule 49 calls the prepositional-predicate copula settled. Every one of the four units names the competing reading under rule 8, and the chapter is internally consistent, so rewriting four hedged edges from outside the verse is not this pass's call; the convention records it so a later chapter can settle it with eyes open.

The ish ish division is uniform here but diverges from precedent in a way a later reader should know: the corpus units where the ASV renders the pair by one expression put that expression on the first token (LEV.15.2 'any man'; EXO.36.4, EZK.14.4, EZK.14.7 'every'), whereas LEV.17, where the ASV writes both a quantifier and a noun, gives the noun plus 'there be' to the first token and the quantifier to the repetition. Those corpus units do not decide the double-rendering case, so this is not an error, but it is recorded.

No promotions and no amendments. The two judgments that would generalise are the copular pronoun, which the corpus contradicts, and the ish ish division, which the corpus does not settle for this shape; a rule the corpus contradicts is worse than none. All three evidence requests were answered, so nothing is outstanding.
